passage:
Everybody yawns. Human babies do it before they are born, and so do dogs, cats, fish and birds. For something so common, it is remarkably poorly understood.

The oldest explanation was that yawning brings in extra oxygen when the blood is short of it. This idea survived for two hundred years and was finally tested in the 1980s. Volunteers were given air with more oxygen than normal, then air with more carbon dioxide. Neither changed how often they yawned. The theory was quietly abandoned.

A newer proposal is that a yawn cools the brain. The jaw stretches wide, which increases blood flow to the head, and the deep breath draws in air that is usually cooler than body temperature. Supporting this, people yawn less when holding something cold against the forehead, and more in warm rooms than in cool ones.

The strangest feature of yawning is that it spreads. Seeing someone yawn, hearing one, or simply reading about yawning makes it more likely that you will do so within a few minutes. This effect is stronger between people who know each other well, and strongest of all between close family members. Children under four are not affected at all, and neither are most children with certain developmental conditions.

That pattern has led researchers to connect contagious yawning with empathy — the capacity to share what another person is feeling. Dogs, which have lived alongside humans for thousands of years, catch yawns from their owners; wolves do not catch them from people. Whatever a yawn was originally for, it appears to have acquired a second job as a signal passed between members of a group.
